name: Retinyl palmitate

lead: Retinyl palmitate is the ester of retinol (vitamin A) with palmitic acid [1]. It is common in over-the-counter skincare, fortified foods and supplements, and is a stable, fat-soluble precursor that the body or skin must convert into active retinoids [1]. Reviews of cosmetic retinoids place it among the first-generation retinoids used in cosmeceuticals, alongside retinol and retinaldehyde [2].

The evidence for its skin benefits is thinner than for tretinoin. A review notes that cosmetic retinoids such as retinol, retinaldehyde and retinyl palmitate are marketed as cosmetics, which do not require clinical efficacy studies, raising concerns about their efficacy [3]. A separate review concluded that retinol, retinyl esters and retinaldehyde in cosmeceuticals are efficacious, safe and well tolerated [2].

paras: In the skin, retinyl esters are thought to be hydrolysed to retinol and converted stepwise to retinoic acid, which acts on retinoid receptors [1][2]. Reviews note that retinoids in cosmetics face problems of instability, low penetration and irritation [3].

A US National Toxicology Program study in mice reported faster tumour development when retinyl palmitate was applied with simulated sunlight; the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel judged it safe in cosmetics up to 3%, and a European committee found no phototoxic potential, according to Grokipedia [1]. High-dose supplement trials such as CARET gave retinyl palmitate with beta-carotene to smokers and asbestos-exposed workers [6]. The injectable medical form carries warnings about overdose and anaphylaxis [7].

lead: Retinyl palmitate is an ester formed between retinol (vitamin A) and palmitic acid (formula C36H60O2), used in cosmetics, fortified foods and dietary supplements as a stable source of vitamin A [1]. In skincare it is grouped among the first-generation retinoids, which also include all-trans retinoic acid, retinol and retinaldehyde, although it is not itself the active form and must be converted in tissue [2][1].

Evidence for cosmetic benefit comes mainly from reviews rather than trials of retinyl palmitate on its own. One 2025 review of cosmetic retinoids in photoaging concluded that retinol, retinyl esters and retinaldehyde used in cosmeceuticals are efficacious, safe and well tolerated, with all-trans retinoic acid regarded as the gold standard [2]. A 2022 review says efficacy concerns exist because clinical studies are not required to market cosmetics, and that retinoids pose formulation challenges (instability, low penetration, irritation) [3].

The compound is also the subject of a public safety controversy over its use in sunscreens and day creams, based on a mouse photocarcinogenicity study. Regulatory and expert panels cited in Grokipedia concluded that it is safe in cosmetics at concentrations up to 3% [1]. In forums it appears in talk of vitamin A intake and as an ingredient some users say they avoid [4][5].

paras: Retinyl palmitate is added to skincare for wrinkles, roughness and hyperpigmentation, positioned as a gentler alternative to prescription retinoids [2][1]. A BMJ Clinical Evidence systematic review of interventions for wrinkles covered interventions to prevent and treat wrinkles and included harms alerts from the FDA and MHRA [6].

As a vitamin A source, retinyl palmitate appears in supplements and fortified foods, and an injectable water-miscible form (Aquasol A) is indicated for vitamin A deficiency when oral administration is not feasible [1][7]. A randomized equivalence trial in Senegalese children with vitamin A deficiency compared retinyl palmitate with beta-carotene and found them statistically equivalent for reversing abnormal eye cytology [8].

Skin. No trial of retinyl palmitate alone against placebo for wrinkles or acne appears in the sources reviewed; the evidence base is reviews of cosmetic retinoids as a group [2][3][6]. A phase 2 trial of retinyl palmitate-loaded ethosomes in facial acne (20 participants) is registered as completed [9].

Nutrition. Retinyl palmitate has been used in trials of vitamin A supplementation, including the Senegal equivalence trial [8]. The Beta-Carotene and Retinol Efficacy Trial (CARET) tested a combination of beta-carotene and vitamin A (as retinyl palmitate) in 18,314 smokers, former smokers and asbestos-exposed workers for effects on lung cancer and cardiovascular disease [10].

Photocarcinogenicity debate. According to Grokipedia, National Toxicology Program studies in SKH-1 hairless mice found that topical retinyl palmitate applied with simulated solar light accelerated squamous cell carcinoma development relative to light alone [1]. The same source says the Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel concluded the ingredient was safe in cosmetics at up to 3%, citing difficulties extrapolating mouse data and the absence of human evidence, and that the European Commission's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety found no phototoxic or photo-irritant potential in vitro or in vivo [1]. A 2017 toxicology publication titled Retinol and Retinyl Palmitate covers the safety assessment of both ingredients [11].

Medical form. The US label for injectable retinyl palmitate warns to avoid overdosage, reports anaphylactic shock and death with the intravenous route, and notes polysorbate-associated E-Ferol syndrome in low-birthweight infants [7].

T Nation threads discuss vitamin A intake from retinyl palmitate in supplements and multivitamins, and one commenter cites retinyl palmitate as a hazardous sunscreen compound when promoting coconut oil as sun protection [4][5][12]. The wiki records these as statements by forum users.
